summary: The developer machine has the core runtime (python, pip), the DocumentDB data-plane MCP server, the Microsoft Learn documentation connector, and a broad set of DocumentDB agent skills installed — enough to start building the Python + LlamaIndex RAG sample against the live cluster. Several cold-answer facts were incorrect or out of date (resource types, CLI commands, connection-string shape, billing model, local dev ports, Entra ID support, vector-index creation syntax). Nothing critical is missing that would block the sample, but a few accelerators and clarifications (embedding model/dimensions, LLM provider, sample data) are absent and should be documented or provided to avoid mistakes.
summary_points: All essential runtime tools for the sample are available: Python 3.13, pip, az (signed-in), node/npx, docker, and the documentdb MCP server.
Key DocumentDB agent skills are installed (deployment, connection, vector-search, indexing, driver guidance), so implementation guidance is on-hand.

Several cold-answer facts were wrong or partly wrong (resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters; CLI group is az documentdb; billing is compute-tier/vCore, not RUs; local gateway uses port 10260), and the builder must not rely on the model memory for these.
Missing accelerators: the DocumentDB Agent Kit listed in the known-accelerators is not present and would speed the build (install with npx).

Information gaps that matter for this sample: which embedding model (provider and dims), which LLM provider and API keys to use, and a canonical sample dataset/seed script — the docs/skills don't decide these.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the Cosmos DB account resource).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB cluster resources are Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (resource type 'mongoClusters').

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-07-01 (deployment-language-terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model recalled the older Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' resource shape (used by Cosmos DB accounts) and conflated Cosmos DB account resources with the vCore-based DocumentDB cluster resource which now uses a dedicated 'mongoClusters' resource type.

confusion_sources.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (naming and history)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for IaC or CLI commands, they would target the wrong resource type and the CLI/Bicep/Terraform calls would fail or manipulate Cosmos DB accounts rather than the vCore mongoClusters resource the sample must use.
improvements: Change quickstarts and agent-kit snippets to use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters when showing vCore-based cluster deployment (Bicep/ARM/Terraform).
Add a short note on the overview pages clarifying that vCore clusters use 'mongoClusters' while legacy Cosmos DB account resources used 'databaseAccounts'.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core Azure CLI group az cosmosdb. Example create command: az cosmosdb create ...
confusions.grounded_answer: The cluster is managed through the az documentdb command group (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create / az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings).

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster (Azure CLI docs)
Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB Mongo API was commonly managed via az cosmosdb; the new vCore product uses az documentdb and a 'mongocluster' subgroup. Shared names (cosmos/db/mongo) caused the model to pick the older command group.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb CLI group (Cosmos DB docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb commands would either operate on a different service (Cosmos DB accounts) or return errors for mongoClusters operations, preventing correct cluster inspection/creation guidance.
improvements: Update CLI quickstarts to use 'az documentdb mongocluster' examples prominently for vCore clusters.
Add an agent-kit lint rule to prefer 'az documentdb' for mongoClusters operations and to warn when 'az cosmosdb' is used in vCore scenarios.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.grounded_answer: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for Bicep/ARM and the corresponding AzAPI/Terraform resource wrappers for mongoClusters (examples and modules reference 'mongoClusters').

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (Bicep & Terraform samples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model defaulted to the Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' resource used historically for Cosmos DB; the newer vCore product uses a new ARM type 'mongoClusters'.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB account ARM/Bicep docs (databaseAccounts)

confusions.build_risk: Bicep or Terraform using the wrong resource type will not create the cluster or will attempt to manage a different resource, wasting time and failing deployment plans.
improvements: Document a short migration note in the 'quickstart-bicep' and 'terraform' pages: vCore clusters use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters, not databaseAccounts.
Add a code-sample snippet at the top of deployment docs that shows the exact Bicep 'mongoClusters' resource.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB clusters provide connection strings from the cluster's Connection strings pane or via az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings; typical client strings use mongodb+srv or mongodb schemes with SCRAM-SHA-256 / OIDC support and the cluster's host (not the legacy *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com Cosmos endpoint). The service also documents that SRV or classic formats are available and that SCRAM-SHA-256 or MONGODB-OIDC can be used depending on auth configuration.

grounding_links.title: Enable private access in Azure DocumentDB (Get connection string to connect)
az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the connection string format used by Cosmos DB Mongo API (host suffix *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com and ports like 10255) rather than the vCore DocumentDB cluster host names and the explicit options DocumentDB docs recommend. Shared 'Mongo-compatible' naming and similar SRV/classic forms made the model conflate the two.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB MongoDB connection strings examples

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix/port or wrong auth mechanism will cause connection failures or insecure configs (e.g., missing TLS flags), leading the sample to fail at the first connection step.
improvements: In the quickstart pages, explicitly show example connection strings for 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore / mongoClusters)' and mark how they differ from 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU)'.

Add a short 'Connection string locator' note in the agent-kit telling agents to use az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings or the portal's Connection strings pane to copy the correct host and auth form.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity for Cosmos DB (DocumentDB) is primarily billed by Request Units (RUs/sec) with options for provisioned throughput, autoscale (RU autoscale), and serverless. There are dedicated vCore-based managed tiers (M-series) in some SKUs.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is billed by compute cluster tier (vCores) and per-GB storage: you pick a cluster tier (M10, M20, M30, etc.) and storage per shard; there are no RUs for this vCore product (RUs apply to Cosmos DB request-unit based offerings).

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model mixed Cosmos DB's RU-based billing (used by Cosmos DB RU-mode accounts) with the vCore-based Azure DocumentDB offer. Both share similar names and are 'Mongo-compatible', causing the confusion.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed RU billing, they might design the sample to set throughput RUs or attempt to use autoscale RU calls that don't exist on the vCore cluster; this wastes time and could lead to incorrect scaling guidance in the sample README.
improvements: Add a clear pricing note at the top of the Azure DocumentDB quickstarts: 'This vCore product bills by cluster tier (M-series) and storage — not RUs'.
Agent-kit snippets that reference billing behavior should branch on product type (vCore vs RU) and use the correct vocabulary.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: The MongoDB-compatible API uses SCRAM username/password (account keys); direct Entra ID token-based data-plane authentication is not commonly supported for the MongoDB wire protocol; management uses Azure AD.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports both Native (SCRAM) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) for data-plane access. Entra ID authentication can be enabled on the cluster (authConfig.allowedModes) and clients can present Entra-issued OIDC tokens to the driver (MONGODB-OIDC mechanism or equivalent callback integration).

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model assumed only the classic SCRAM/key mechanism common to older Cosmos/Mongo endpoints. Recent product updates add Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) data-plane auth; the model's memory missed that capability.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Entra ID isn't supported they may hardcode keys or refuse to implement OIDC token flows; conversely, if they assume Entra ID is default, they may not include fallback to native SCRAM. Both lead to auth failures in different clusters.
improvements: Add a short 'Authentication' section to the quickstart that shows both forms (native SCRAM and Entra ID) with minimal example code and az/portal steps to enable Entra ID on a cluster.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers for data plane (for Python use pymongo). There is no separate service-specific data-plane SDK; management uses Azure management SDKs.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for Python) for data-plane operations; management/ARM tasks use Azure management SDKs (azure-resourcemanager packages).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Modern vector-capable clusters advertise HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. Example createIndex: db.documents.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { vector: { dims: 1536, method: 'hnsw', metric: 'cosine' } }).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector index kinds vector-hnsw, vector-ivf (IVF), and vector-diskann; creation uses the database runCommand form (createIndexes) or index APIs with cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions specifying kind, dimensions and algorithm-specific options (m, efConstruction for HNSW; numLists for IVF; maxDegree/lBuild for DiskANN). The $search aggregation stage (cosmosSearch) queries the vector index.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB
Build RAG applications (create a vector index)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer named the correct algorithms but suggested a generic createIndex syntax that isn't the documented form for Azure DocumentDB's cosmosSearch vector indexes; the product exposes specialized options (cosmosSearchOptions) that differ from the simple 'vector' index spec the model invented.

confusion_sources.title: Community or generic vector createIndex examples (non-Azure)

confusions.build_risk: If builder uses the wrong index creation syntax the createIndex call will fail or create a different index type, preventing vector queries from working in the sample.
improvements: Show exact createIndexes/runCommand examples for each vector kind (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN) on the vector-search docs landing page and include a one-line pymongo runCommand snippet.
Add an example in the agent-kit that maps common embedding dims -> index kind recommendations (small demo: HNSW on M30, DiskANN for >500K docs).

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text search is normally done using Azure Cognitive Search integrated with Cosmos DB, or by built-in text indexing if available; hybrid is implemented by combining Azure Cognitive Search with vector results in the application.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB offers a built-in BM25 full-text engine (preview via createSearchIndexes and $search) and an integrated vector store (cosmosSearch). Hybrid retrieval is supported server-side by running two searches (BM25 and vector) and fusing results (Reciprocal Rank Fusion) in a single aggregation pipeline (server-side $unionWith fusion or client-side fusion). No separate Azure Cognitive Search is required for hybrid scenarios.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB
Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model defaulted to a common architecture (Azure Cognitive Search + external vector DB) rather than the integrated DocumentDB full-text + vector search facility described in the product docs. Similar names and overlapping Azure search offerings lead to the mix-up.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cognitive Search + Cosmos DB integration guidance (older patterns)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses Azure Cognitive Search instead of the built-in createSearchIndexes/cosmosSearch path, the sample will be more complex and will not demonstrate the product's integrated hybrid capability. Extra infra and costs would be introduced unnecessarily.
improvements: Make the built-in hybrid examples (createSearchIndexes + cosmosSearch + RRF) the primary pattern in the 'build RAG applications' docs so agents use the integrated approach by default.
Add a one-paragraph 'Don't use Cognitive Search for this sample' note in LlamaIndex/agent-kit snippets when targeting DocumentDB.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supports recent wire protocol versions (4.x - 7.0) and some features differ: some admin commands, server-side JS and certain aggregation operators may be limited.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0, and 8.0 across supported tiers and documents the differences in the compatibility reference; it supports most MongoDB features but some admin commands and specific commands are not exposed for managed PaaS reasons (see the compatibility doc for exact operator support).

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Run a local mongo:7 official image on port 27017; there's no perfect emulator that matches DocumentDB cloud behaviour.
confusions.grounded_answer: For local development the recommended gateway Docker image is ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest (the DocumentDB gateway) and it exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 (and PostgreSQL on 9712). The documents and local deployment skill instruct connecting with TLS and SCRAM-SHA-256 and using env-driven config for tlsRelaxation and ports.

grounding_links.title: documentdb-local-deployment

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model assumed a generic MongoDB image (mongo:7) and the common 27017 port usually used for standalone MongoDB, but Azure DocumentDB provides its own Gateway image with a different default port (10260) for parity with the cloud product.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder runs a generic mongo: image and tests against it, vector and DocumentDB-specific features (cosmosSearch, createSearchIndexes, DiskANN/HNSW options) will not be present and the sample's integration tests will fail or be misleading.
improvements: Make the local Gateway Docker command and port (10260) the first example in local-deployment docs and quickstarts to avoid the default 27017 assumption.
Add a short 'Do not use mongo:latest for DocumentDB feature testing' note in sample READMEs.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams may be available depending on the account's MongoDB wire-protocol compatibility level and cluster SKU; if supported you can use watch(); some accounts historically did not support change streams or required replica-set configuration.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported in Azure DocumentDB. For multishard clusters some preview features must be enabled (Change streams for multishard clusters). The docs provide examples and explain resumability and preview gating for multi-shard scenarios.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model hedged because change-stream support historically varied across offerings and tiers; the product now documents change-stream support and flags the extra step for multishard clusters.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are not supported they might implement more complex polling or miss out on efficient online migration / streaming scenarios; if they assume multishard change streams are enabled by default they may fail on clusters where the preview flag isn't turned on.
improvements: Add a short 'enablement note' to change-streams doc indicating when the multishard preview must be enabled and how to do it (portal/az/resource patch example).

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: The service-specific MCP server is 'documentdb' and the general azure MCP server does not provide the same data-plane index tooling — use the documentdb MCP server.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server provides data-plane tools (list_databases, create_index, explain, aggregate, etc.), and although azure MCP exists for control-plane operations, the documentdb server is the right one for collection/index/query inspection.
confusions.grounding_source: machine inventory (documentdb MCP server listed) and the documentdb MCP tool descriptions

grounding_links.title: documentdb

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft originally shipped a service called DocumentDB which evolved into Azure Cosmos DB; Cosmos DB exposes multiple APIs. This service is Microsoft-managed Cosmos DB offering a MongoDB-compatible endpoint; it is not the same as unrelated open-source 'documentdb'.
confusions.grounded_answer: The naming is nuanced: the vCore offering was previously named 'vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB' and was renamed 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)'. It is distinct from the original 2014-2017 'DocumentDB' (which became Cosmos DB) and separate from Amazon DocumentDB. The service is also aligned with the open-source DocumentDB engine (DocumentDB on GitHub) that powers this offering.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The product history and overlapping names (DocumentDB, Cosmos DB, Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB) create natural confusion, but docs now clarify the distinctions.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath is Azure Cosmos DB exposing the MongoDB wire protocol; application code should use standard MongoDB drivers but validate advanced features.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (DocumentDB project) built on PostgreSQL and exposes the MongoDB wire protocol. Applications should use standard MongoDB drivers, but must validate advanced operations against DocumentDB compatibility docs because some admin commands or provider-specific features differ. This is not the Azure Cosmos DB engine.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance
DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model conflated Cosmos DB's managed engine with the new vCore DocumentDB offering because both provide MongoDB-compatible endpoints and similar developer experiences.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming the Cosmos DB engine is underneath could lead a builder to adopt Cosmos-specific admin guidance or expect RU billing and Cosmos-specific endpoints; this can break integration or lead to wrong provisioning choices.
improvements: Add a short 'engine and compatibility' note in the product overview pages that explicitly states 'Azure DocumentDB is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (Postgres-based) and is not the underlying engine for Azure Cosmos DB'.
Agent kit examples should show both: 'If target is DocumentDB (vCore) use mongoClusters and DocumentDB docs; if target is Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) use cosmosdb account APIs and RU docs.'

confusions.question: What index definition will the sample create for vector search (shape and create command)?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field called 'embedding' with a HNSW method. Example: db.regulatory_docs.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { vector: { dims: 1536, method: 'hnsw', metric: 'cosine' } }).
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the documented createIndexes/runCommand pattern with 'key' pointing to the vector path and 'cosmosSearchOptions' (or kind: 'vector-hnsw') to specify algorithm and parameters. Example (createIndexes with cosmosSearchOptions / kind vector-hnsw) and specify dims and algorithm-specific parameters (m, efConstruction for HNSW).

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (HNSW example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model produced a simplified generic createIndex example not matching DocumentDB's documented cosmosSearchOptions/createIndexes syntax.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong index creation API will fail or create an incompatible index and the vector search calls in the sample will not return results.
improvements: Show a copy-paste-ready runCommand JSON example in the quickstart for creating vector indexes with dims and algorithm options for HNSW/IVF/DiskANN.

information_gaps.title: Embedding model and vector dimension
information_gaps.description: The sample prompt does not specify which embedding model (provider, family, or exact model) to use and therefore the vector dimension (dims) for index creation is unknown. I searched Microsoft Learn, the installed skills and quickstarts for guidance but those only say 'set dims to your model output size'. The builder needs to decide and record the embedding model and dims (e.g., OpenAI text-embedding-3 = 1536) before creating vector indexes.

information_gaps.title: LLM provider and API keys (embedding/LLM)
information_gaps.description: The prompt does not specify which LLM or embeddings provider to use (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, local Llama, Hugging Face, etc.) or the env var names. None of the DocumentDB skills pick an embedding/LLM provider — they only show how to store/query vectors. The builder must select provider(s) and document which env vars to set (e.g., OPENAI_API_KEY or AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT/KEY).

information_gaps.title: Canonical sample dataset & seed script
information_gaps.description: The prompt requires indexing 'regulatory documents' and 'internal policy documents' but provides no dataset. The skills discuss sample-data management patterns but no canonical seed set is provided. The builder needs a small synthetic dataset or a seeded loader script (what fields, metadata, and the shape of documents).

information_gaps.title: App surface (CLI vs HTTP vs both)
information_gaps.description: The prompt implies an analyze flow but doesn't mandate CLI or HTTP API surface. The docs/skills don't prescribe a UI surface for LlamaIndex samples. Builder must decide whether to implement a CLI, HTTP endpoint (FastAPI/Flask), or both and document that choice.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the ARM/resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (CLI group 'az documentdb mongocluster' and the 'mongoClusters' Bicep/Terraform resource) for any control-plane or IaC operations targeting the vCore DocumentDB offering.

Provision indexes for vector search using the documented createIndexes/runCommand pattern and 'cosmosSearchOptions' (or 'kind' values vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, vector-diskann), and set 'dimensions' to your chosen embedding model's output size (do not use a generic createIndex signature).
